reading_text:
The Workers' World
Name ______________________Date ______________Period __________
The Workers' World
Directions: Read the full text, then answer the questions at the end.
The New Factory Discipline
Industrial work ran on the clock. A factory whistle set the start of the day, bells marked the breaks, and foremen enforced a pace set by machines rather than by the worker. Ten to twelve hours a day, six days a week, was a common schedule, and some steelworkers worked periodic 24-hour turns.
The work was also dangerous. Unguarded belts and gears, mine gas, and molten metal killed and maimed workers in large numbers each year. There was no workers' compensation system, and courts commonly held that a worker who accepted a dangerous job had accepted its risks.
Wages, and the Children Who Had to Work
Pay was low and unsteady. Average yearly earnings for manufacturing workers were on the order of a few hundred dollars, and layoffs could cut even that away without warning. A single adult wage often could not cover rent, food, and clothing. Families closed the gap the only way open to them: more members went to work.
That arithmetic put children into the mills. The census of 1900 counted about 1.75 million children ages 10 to 15 in paid work, roughly one child in five. They tended spinning frames, sorted slate from coal in mines, and worked in glass factories, canneries, and street trades. Employers valued them because they were cheap, could reach into small spaces around machinery, and rarely protested. Most left school early. Child labor was one of the ways the system balanced its books, by paying adults less than a family needed to live.
Why Workers Combined
A single worker who asked for higher wages or a shorter day could simply be replaced. Alone, workers had no bargaining power. Together they might. A union let workers negotiate as a group, a practice called collective bargaining, and a strike, the refusal to work, gave the group its leverage: if all the spinners stopped at once, production stopped with them.
Employers resisted organization itself. Companies fired union members, circulated blacklists of organizers, required pledges not to join a union, and hired replacement workers during strikes.
Two Roads: The Knights and the AFL
The Knights of Labor, founded in 1869 and led in the 1880s by Terence Powderly, took the broad road. The Knights organized many kinds of workers in the same order: skilled and unskilled, factory hands and farmers, and, unusually for the time, many women and Black workers. Their program reached beyond wages to broad reform: the eight-hour day, the end of child labor, and eventual worker ownership of industry. Membership surged after successful railroad strikes in 1885, to roughly 700,000 by some contemporary estimates in 1886.
The American Federation of Labor, founded in 1886 under Samuel Gompers, took the narrower road. The AFL was a federation of craft unions, each organizing one skilled trade, such as cigarmakers, iron molders, or carpenters. It concentrated on wages, hours, and working conditions, and built unions with dues and strike funds meant to survive a long fight.
Three Defeats
On May 4, 1886, during a national campaign for the eight-hour day, a Chicago labor meeting in Haymarket Square was ending when police moved in to disperse it. Someone, never identified, threw a bomb into the police ranks. The blast and gunfire killed seven police officers and at least four civilians, by the counts most often given; totals differ across accounts. Eight anarchist leaders were tried for murder on the theory that their speeches had encouraged the act. Four were hanged. No evidence connected any of them to the bomb itself. In the public mind, labor and violence were now linked. The Knights of Labor, who had not called the meeting, were blamed too, and their membership collapsed within a few years.
At Homestead, Pennsylvania, in 1892, the issue was union survival itself. Henry Clay Frick, running the Carnegie Steel works while Andrew Carnegie was in Scotland, set out to break the union and cut wages. When the contract expired, Frick locked the workers out and brought in about 300 armed Pinkerton guards by barge. Workers met them in a day-long gun battle on July 6 in which about ten men died, by the counts most often given; totals differ. The Pinkertons surrendered. The victory lasted days. Pennsylvania sent some 8,000 militia, the plant reopened with replacement workers under military protection, and the strike collapsed by November. Steel remained largely unorganized for a generation.
The Pullman strike of 1894 began in a company town. George Pullman cut wages at his railroad car works near Chicago during the depression of the 1890s but did not cut the rents in his company town. His workers struck in May 1894 and appealed to Eugene V. Debs and the American Railway Union, which voted to boycott all trains carrying Pullman cars, tying up rail traffic across much of the country. A federal court issued an injunction ordering the union to stop interfering with the trains and the mail, and President Cleveland sent federal troops to Chicago over the governor's objection. About thirty people died in clashes, by the estimate most often given; counts differ. Debs was jailed for violating the injunction, the union was destroyed, and the strike ended in defeat.
The pattern across the three defeats is the lesson. Employers hired private guards, replacement workers, and lawyers. Governments supplied militia, troops, and court orders. Newspapers commonly presented strikers as dangerous radicals, turning public opinion against them. Unions that stretched beyond what their members and funds could hold broke under the strain. The AFL's narrower unions survived.
Questions
1. According to the reading, why did so many children work for pay in 1900? Give two reasons, one about families and one about employers.
2. How did the Knights of Labor and the American Federation of Labor differ in whom they organized and in what they tried to win?
3. At Homestead, the workers won the battle on July 6, 1892, and lost the strike. Explain how both halves of that sentence are true.
4. What role did courts and the federal government play in ending the Pullman strike? Name the legal tool used and what happened to Eugene V. Debs.
5. The reading argues that strike defeats followed a pattern. State the pattern in your own words, then support it with one specific fact from each of the three defeats.
Teacher Answer Key
1. According to the reading, why did so many children work for pay in 1900? Give two reasons, one about families and one about employers. Family reason: a single adult wage, on the order of a few hundred dollars a year and subject to layoffs, often could not cover rent, food, fuel, and clothing, so families needed children's earnings to survive. Employer reason: children were cheap, could reach into small spaces around machinery, and rarely protested, so employers actively valued and hired them. The census of 1900 counted about 1.75 million working children ages 10 to 15, roughly one in five.
2. How did the Knights of Labor and the American Federation of Labor differ in whom they organized and in what they tried to win? The Knights organized many kinds of workers in one order, skilled and unskilled, and many women and Black workers, and pursued broad reform: the eight-hour day, an end to child labor, and eventually worker ownership of industry. The AFL was a federation of separate craft unions, each organizing one skilled trade, and concentrated on wages, hours, and working conditions won through collective bargaining, supported by dues and strike funds.
3. At Homestead, the workers won the battle on July 6, 1892, and lost the strike. Explain how both halves of that sentence are true. Won the battle: workers fought the roughly 300 Pinkerton guards Frick brought in by barge in a day-long gun battle and forced their surrender. Lost the strike: Pennsylvania sent some 8,000 militia, the works reopened with replacement workers under military protection, and the strike collapsed by November. The union was destroyed at Homestead and steel stayed largely unorganized for a generation. Winning against a private force did not help once the state supplied the force instead.
4. What role did courts and the federal government play in ending the Pullman strike? Name the legal tool used and what happened to Eugene V. Debs. A federal court issued an injunction ordering the American Railway Union to stop interfering with trains and the mail, and President Cleveland sent federal troops to Chicago over the Illinois governor's objection. Debs defied the injunction and was jailed for violating it. The union was destroyed and the strike ended in complete defeat.
5. The reading argues that strike defeats followed a pattern. State the pattern in your own words, then support it with one specific fact from each of the three defeats. Pattern: employers combined private force, replacement workers, and legal action; governments supplied troops, militia, and court orders; newspapers linked labor with violence and turned public opinion; and unions that overextended broke, while narrower, better funded unions survived. Accept any accurate fact per case. Haymarket: the bomb thrower was never identified, yet eight leaders were tried, four hanged, and the Knights, who had not called the meeting, were blamed and collapsed. Homestead: Pinkertons surrendered, but state militia reopened the plant with replacements and the strike collapsed. Pullman: a federal injunction, federal troops, and Debs jailed ended the boycott and destroyed the American Railway Union.

Guided Notes: The Workers' World
Name ______________________Date ______________Period __________
Guided Notes: The Workers' World
Lesson question: Why did workers organize, and why did collective action so often end in defeat?
Unit question: How did industrial growth transform American life, and who gained, who paid, and who resisted?
Key Terms
union: an organization of workers formed to bargain with employers as a group
strike: a work stoppage meant to pressure an employer to meet workers' demands
collective bargaining: negotiation between an employer and workers organized as a group
injunction: a court order that requires or forbids a specific action
Knights of Labor: a national labor organization of the 1870s and 1880s that sought broad reform and organized many kinds of workers
American Federation of Labor: a federation of craft unions founded in 1886 that focused on wages, hours, and working conditions
child labor: paid work by children, often in factories, mines, mills, and street trades
A. The Factory Day
A normal industrial schedule was (1) ____________ to ____________ hours a day, ____________ days a week. The pace of work was set by (2) ____________, enforced by foremen, not by the worker. A worker injured on the job had no (3) ____________, and courts usually held that the worker had accepted the ____________ of the job.
B. Wages and Child Labor
Average yearly earnings for manufacturing workers were on the order of (4) ____________ dollars, and one adult wage often could not cover (5) ____________, ____________, and clothing for a family. The census of 1900 counted about (6) ____________ children ages 10 to 15 in paid work, about one child in ____________. Employers hired children because they were (7) ____________, could reach into small spaces, and rarely protested.
C. Why Workers Combined
One worker alone had no (8) ____________ power, because one worker could simply be ____________. Organized as a group, workers could practice (9) ____________ and back it with a strike. Employers answered by firing union members, circulating (10) ____________ of organizers, and hiring ____________ workers during strikes.
D. Two Roads
The Knights of Labor, led by (11) ____________, organized many kinds of workers in one order and sought ____________ reform, including the eight-hour day and an end to child labor. Membership reached roughly (12) ____________ in 1886.
The American Federation of Labor, founded in (13) ____________ and led by Samuel Gompers, was a federation of ____________ unions. It focused on (14) ____________, ____________, and working conditions, and built strike funds so its unions could survive a long fight.
E. Three Defeats
Haymarket, Chicago, 1886. During the campaign for the (15) ____________ day, a bomb was thrown at police in Haymarket Square. The person who threw it was (16) ____________. Eight leaders were tried and (17) ____________ were hanged. The Knights were blamed, and their membership ____________.
Homestead, Pennsylvania, 1892. (18) ____________, running the Carnegie Steel works, locked the workers out and brought in about 300 (19) ____________ guards by barge. The workers won the battle on July 6, but Pennsylvania sent the (20) ____________, the plant reopened with replacement workers, and the strike collapsed.
Pullman, 1894. George Pullman cut (21) ____________ but not the rents in his company town. The American Railway Union, led by (22) ____________, boycotted trains carrying Pullman cars. A federal court issued an (23) ____________, President Cleveland sent federal ____________, and Debs was ____________.
The Three Defeats at a Glance
Strike
What the workers wanted
Why it ended in defeat
Haymarket 1886
Homestead 1892
Pullman 1894
Exit Ticket
1. In your own words, why did workers organize into unions in this period? Give two reasons from the lesson.
2. Choose one of the three defeats. Name the force, other than the employer, that helped defeat the workers, and explain how it was used.
3. The AFL survived the 1890s while the Knights of Labor collapsed. Give one reason from the lesson that explains the difference.
Teacher Answer Key
(1) 10; 12; six
(2) machines
(3) workers' compensation; risks
(4) a few hundred
(5) rent; food (fuel also acceptable)
(6) 1.75 million; five
(7) cheap
(8) bargaining; replaced
(9) collective bargaining
(10) blacklists; replacement
(11) Terence Powderly; broad
(12) 700,000
(13) 1886; craft
(14) wages; hours
(15) eight-hour
(16) never identified
(17) four
(18) Henry Clay Frick
(19) Pinkerton
(20) state militia (about 8,000)
(21) wages
(22) Eugene V. Debs
(23) injunction; troops; jailed (imprisoned)
At a glance, Haymarket: wanted the eight-hour day; defeated because the bomb linked labor with violence in public opinion, leaders were tried and hanged, and the Knights were blamed and collapsed.
At a glance, Homestead: wanted to keep their union and stop a wage cut; defeated because state militia protected the reopened plant and replacement workers until the strike collapsed.
At a glance, Pullman: wanted wages restored or rents lowered and union recognition; defeated because a federal injunction and federal troops broke the boycott and Debs was jailed.
Exit ticket 1: accept any two of low wages that could not support a family, long hours and machine-set pace, dangerous work with no compensation, and the fact that a single worker could be replaced at will. Exit ticket 2: Haymarket, public opinion and the courts; Homestead, the state militia; Pullman, the federal injunction, federal troops, or the courts. Exit ticket 3: the AFL organized narrower craft unions, focused on wages, hours, and conditions, and kept dues and strike funds, so it did not overextend the way the Knights did.
